title: Climate suitability change predicted little of US bird abundance change in 2010-2025: 0.05 per log unit within species on survey routes, and no species-level forecast skill
abstract: Stephens et al. (2016) reported that climate suitability trends predict bird population trends. We tested this forward in time with the US Breeding Bird Survey (2026 release, 1966-2025) and nClimGrid monthly climate. We fitted one Poisson climate model for each of 367 species to its 1981-2000 distribution on 2,690 routes (346 species with spatial-block AUC 0.7 or more) and kept the models frozen. We compared suitability change with abundance change in 1981-2009 and in a forward period 2010-2025, in the East and the West, with observer controls. Within species, abundance change between 2010-14 and 2021-25 followed suitability change on 1,623 routes: 0.053 log units per log unit (95% CI 0.035 to 0.070), East 0.061, West 0.036. The result stayed positive with species x region fixed effects, same-observer routes, a boosted-tree model and US-centred species, and it followed 2010-2025 suitability change, not 1981-2009 change. In 1981-2009 the within-species link was weaker and not robust. Between species, suitability trends did not predict population trends in 1981-2009 (Spearman -0.01) and only weakly in 2010-2025 (0.085, p = 0.11); a model calibrated on 1981-2009 had no forecast skill for 2010-2025. Species suitability trends were not stable between periods (Spearman 0.03). Observer fixed effects made the median 2010-2025 trend more negative (-0.134 versus -0.050 log per decade). Limitations: US-only climate models cut cross-border ranges, the models have four climate variables and no land cover, suitability errors reduce the coefficient, and BBS counts do not model detection.
